title: Man'oushe
skill: Shaping a yeast dough into flatbreads

notes.2: Makes 16. Knead the dough in two halves.

move.title: Kneaded, dimpled, baked hot
move.body: Man'oushe is the Lebanese breakfast flatbread, sold warm from bakeries and made at home on weekend mornings. It starts from the same lean dough as pita. Today you'll bloom the yeast at 105 to 110°F, knead the dough to a windowpane, and press dimples into each round so it bakes flat under its za'atar and olive oil instead of puffing.

callback.body: Pita's rounds puffed into pockets in a very hot oven. Man'oushe is that dough again, but pressed full of dimples, so the steam escapes and the bread stays flat under its topping.

why.title: 105 to 110°F
why.body: Yeast is alive. Water at 105 to 110°F wakes it up gently; above about 130°F starts to kill it, and cold water leaves it sleepy. The foam on top tells you it's working.

why.title: Kneaded to a windowpane
why.body: Kneading lines up the gluten into a stretchy net. When a small piece stretches thin enough to see light through, the net is strong enough to roll thin without tearing.

why.title: Why the balls rest
why.body: Dividing and rounding tightens the gluten, so the dough springs back. Ten minutes under a towel relaxes it, and it rolls out easily and stays round.

why.title: Dimples keep it flat
why.body: Pressing your fingertips into the dough pops the big bubbles and seals the layers together, so it can't puff into a pocket. The dimples also hold little pools of za'atar and oil.

why.title: A very hot pan
why.body: A pan heated upside down in a 475°F oven bakes the bottom fast and crisp, before the topping can burn.

wrong.fix: The water was too hot or the yeast was old. Start again with fresh yeast and water at 105 to 110°F.

wrong.sign: A round keeps shrinking back as you roll it
wrong.fix: Leave it under the towel 5 more minutes and roll it again.

wrong.sign: One puffed up like a pita
wrong.fix: Press the dimples deeper, all the way to the counter, on the next ones.
Leave a little more oil on top, and take them out as soon as the edges turn golden.

quiz.q: What water temperature wakes up the yeast?
quiz.explain: Above about 130°F starts to kill it.

quiz.q: What does the windowpane test show?
choices: The gluten is strong enough to roll thin
quiz.explain: The dough stretches thin enough to see light through.

quiz.q: Why press dimples into the dough?
choices: So it bakes flat instead of puffing into a pocket
quiz.explain: The dimples let the steam escape.

ingredients.text: a little more, for the bowl

substitutions.note: Mix 2 tablespoons of dried thyme, 1 tablespoon of sesame seeds, 1 tablespoon of sumac, and ½ teaspoon of salt.

steps.text: Warm the water in the measuring cup in the microwave for about 30 seconds. Stir it and check it with the thermometer: 105 to 110°F.
steps.tip: Too hot? Let it sit a minute and check again.

steps.text: Pour the water into the large bowl. Stir in the sugar, then sprinkle the yeast over the top and leave it alone to bloom.
steps.look: A layer of foam on top, and it smells like bread.

steps.text: Add the flour, salt, and 2 tablespoons of oil. Stir with the wooden spoon until a rough, shaggy dough forms.
steps.tip: Don't taste the raw dough. Raw flour can make you sick.

steps.text: Dust the counter with flour and turn the dough out. Knead it until it's smooth and stretchy, then do the windowpane test. If it tears, knead 2 more minutes and test again.
steps.look: A small piece stretches thin enough to see light through without tearing.

steps.text: Rub a little oil around the bowl, put the dough in, and turn it once to coat it. Cover with the towel and leave it somewhere warm until it doubles.
steps.look: Doubled. A floured finger pressed in leaves a dent that stays.

steps.text: Put the sheet pan upside down on the lowest rack and heat the oven to 475°F.
Weigh the dough and divide the weight by 8. Cut 8 pieces of that weight with the knife and roll each into a smooth ball. Cover them with the towel.
Stir the za'atar and the ⅓ cup of olive oil together in the small bowl. Slice the tomatoes and cucumber into ¼-inch rounds.
Roll 2 balls into rounds 7 inches across and ¼ inch thick. Press your fingertips straight down all over each round, all the way to the counter, leaving a ½-inch rim.
steps.look: Dimples close together over the whole round, with a plain rim.

steps.text: Stir the topping and spread about 1 tablespoon over each round with the back of the spoon, out to the rim.
With oven mitts, pull the rack out partway. Slide the rounds onto the hot pan with the spatula, push the rack back in, and close the door. Bake until the edges are golden.
steps.look: Golden edges, and the bottoms have brown spots.

steps.text: Lift them out with the spatula onto the cutting board. Roll, dimple, top, and bake the rest the same way, 2 at a time. Turn off the oven when the last ones are out.
Lay tomato, cucumber, and a few mint leaves on each warm man'oushe and fold or roll it up to eat.
